read.sections.0.heading.back: A court that crosses today's borders

read.sections.0.text.source:
The Mughal dynasty, a family of rulers, began in 1526 with Babur, a Muslim prince from Central Asia. Across different reigns, Mughal lands included Kabul, Lahore, Agra, Delhi and Bengal. These places are now in Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. The empire's borders changed over time. This history belongs to a connected South Asia that crossed today's national borders. A court was the ruler's household, with the officials, advisers and workers around him. It was a centre of government, wealth and work for artists.

Akbar, emperor from 1556 to 1605, became an important patron, someone who supports or orders art. His painters included people from Iran, and from Hindu and Muslim communities in South Asia. Together they helped build a Mughal style that kept changing. These labels describe some of the painters' connections. They do not mean that everyone from one religion or region painted in the same way. Artists learned from one another. They made choices for particular commissions, or ordered works.
read.sections.0.text.note: Rulers (Babur, Akbar, Shah Jahan) are referred to as พระองค์ and Jahangir as พระโอรส, the usual school forms; KEY_TERMS asks for plain royal words, so check the level. People's names stay in Latin letters per the brief. court as ราชสำนัก; officials as ข้าราชการ; 'commissions, or ordered works' as การสั่งทำแต่ละครั้งหรืองานที่มีคนสั่งให้ทำ.
read.sections.0.text.back:
The Mughal dynasty, or ruling family, began in 1526 with Babur, a Muslim prince from Central Asia. In different reigns, Mughal lands included Kabul, Lahore, Agra, Delhi and Bengal. Today these places are in Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. The empire's borders changed over time. This history belongs to a South Asia connected across today's national borders. A court was the ruler's household, including the officials, advisers and workers around him. The court was a centre of government, wealth and artists' work.

Akbar, emperor from 1556 to 1605, became an important patron, someone who supports or commissions art. His painters included people from Iran and people from Hindu and Muslim communities in South Asia. Together they created a Mughal style that kept changing. These group names tell some of the painters' connections; they don't mean everyone from the same religion or region painted the same way. Artists learned from each other and made choices for each commission, or work someone ordered.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
The Mughals were a family of rulers. The first, Babur, began to rule in 1526. He was a Muslim prince from Central Asia. At different times, Mughal lands included Kabul, Lahore, Agra, Delhi and Bengal. Today they are in Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. A court was the ruler's home, with his officials and workers. It ran the government. It held great wealth. It gave work to artists.

Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605. He was an important patron. A patron pays for art or asks for it. Some of his painters came from Iran. Others came from Hindu and Muslim groups in South Asia. Together they made a Mughal style. It kept changing. But people from one group did not all paint the same way. Artists learned from each other.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
The Mughal dynasty was a ruling family. The first ruler was Babur. He began ruling in 1526. He was a Muslim prince from Central Asia. At different times, Mughal lands included Kabul, Lahore, Agra, Delhi and Bengal. Today these places are in Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. A court was the ruler's home, including officials and workers. The court ran the government, had great wealth and gave work to artists.

Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605. He was an important patron. A patron is someone who pays for or asks for art to be made. Some painters came from Iran. Some came from Hindu and Muslim groups in South Asia. Together they created a Mughal style. This style kept changing. But people from the same group did not all paint the same way. Artists learned from each other.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The royal House of Books was both a library and a workshop. There, specialists made books by hand. Painters worked alongside calligraphers, decorators and bookbinders. Master artists from Iran helped direct the work. In some paintings, one artist planned the composition, others added colour, and specialists painted faces or animals. Akbar also ordered translations into Persian of works in Sanskrit, an ancient South Asian language. They included the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, two famous long poems. These projects connected languages and beliefs. They also displayed the emperor's learning and wealth.

Later patrons valued albums: bound collections of single paintings and examples of beautiful handwriting. The Shah Jahan Album was begun under Akbar's son Jahangir, and more was added under Shah Jahan. This practice linked Mughal collecting with earlier album traditions in Iran and in the Timurid world of Central Asia. An album could place works from different generations on newly decorated pages. Its unity came from collecting, mounting and arranging pages, not only from making new pictures.
read.sections.1.text.note: House of Books as หอหนังสือ; album as อัลบั้ม (glossary); calligraphy and calligraphers as อักษรวิจิตร / นักอักษรวิจิตร (also used in AAS02). Mahabharata and Ramayana as มหาภารตะ and รามายณะ, Timurid as ราชวงศ์ติมูริด, Sanskrit สันสกฤต. 'These projects' rendered งานแปลเหล่านี้ to keep โครงการ out of the text.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The court's book house was both a library and a workshop. There specialists made books by hand. Painters worked with calligraphers, decorators and bookbinders. Master artists from Iran helped direct the work. In some paintings, one artist planned the composition, others painted the colour, and specialists painted faces or animals. Akbar also ordered works in Sanskrit, an ancient language of South Asia, translated into Persian. Those works included the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, two famous long poems. These translations connected languages and beliefs, and also showed the emperor's learning and wealth.

Later patrons valued albums, books binding together single paintings and examples of beautiful handwriting. The Shah Jahan Album was begun under Jahangir, Akbar's son, and added to under Shah Jahan. This practice connected Mughal collecting with album-making traditions that existed earlier in Iran and in the Timurid world of Central Asia. An album could place works by different generations on newly decorated pages. Its unity came from collecting, mounting and arranging pages, not only from making new pictures.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Akbar's House of Books was a library and a workshop. Experts made books there by hand. Painters worked with writers, decorators and people who bound books. Master artists from Iran led the work. Sometimes one artist planned a picture. Others added colour. Experts painted the faces or animals. Akbar had famous poems put into Persian. They were in Sanskrit, an old South Asian language. Two were the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. These books linked languages and beliefs. They showed the ruler's learning and wealth.

Later rulers loved albums. An album is a book of chosen paintings and fine writing. The Shah Jahan Album was begun by Jahangir, Akbar's son. Shah Jahan added more to it. Rulers in Iran and Central Asia made albums first. An album could put old and new works together. New borders were painted around them.

read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Akbar's book house was both a library and a workshop. Specialists made books by hand there. Painters worked with letter writers, decorators and bookbinders. Master artists from Iran led the work. Sometimes one artist planned the picture, others painted the colour, and specialists painted faces or animals. Akbar had famous poems translated into Persian. These poems were written in Sanskrit, an old language of South Asia. Two of them were the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. These books joined languages and beliefs. They showed the ruler's learning and wealth.

Later rulers liked albums very much. An album is a book that collects chosen paintings and beautiful handwriting. The Shah Jahan Album was begun by Jahangir, the son of Akbar, the earlier ruler. Later Shah Jahan added more work. Rulers in Iran and Central Asia made albums before. One album could bring old and new work together. New borders were painted around them.

read.sections.2.text.source:
In Chitarman's portrait, dated 1627–28, Shah Jahan stands on a terrace. He holds a pendant that contains a small picture of himself. Jewels, patterned clothing and a shining halo around his head stress his rank. Small angels hovering above draw on European pictures. This is a carefully built royal image. Its luxury also stands for the skills of the many makers who supplied the court. They included weavers and jewellers. Artistic connections travelled along more than one route and across more than one border.

Another album page surrounds flowing calligraphy, or skilled decorative writing, with plants and grazing animals. Its calligraphy is credited to Mir 'Ali Haravi, who is linked with Herat, now in Afghanistan. The writing dates to about 1535–45; the decoration around it probably belongs to the seventeenth century. Treasuring an older work and giving it a new setting joined artistic histories across time. Both pages show the court's interests and wealth. They do not show every person's life across the empire.
read.sections.2.text.note: European angels as ทูตสวรรค์ (not เทวดา, which suggests Hindu-Buddhist deities): check. Herat as เฮรัต. pendant as จี้; halo as รัศมี.
read.sections.2.text.back:
In Chitarman's portrait, dated 1627–28, Shah Jahan stands on a terrace. He holds a pendant with a small picture of himself inside. Jewels, patterned clothing and a shining halo around his head stress his status. Small angels floating above are modelled on European pictures. This is a deliberately made image of a king. The luxury in the picture also stands for the skill of many makers who supplied the court, including weavers and jewellers. Artistic connections travelled along more than one route and across more than one border.

The other album page surrounds flowing calligraphy, or skilful decorative writing, with plants and grazing animals. The calligraphy is attributed to Mir 'Ali Haravi, who is associated with Herat in present-day Afghanistan. The writing dates to about 1535–45, while the surrounding decoration probably comes from the 17th century. Treasuring an old work and giving it a new home joins art histories across time. Both pages show the court's interests and wealth, not the lives of everyone across the empire.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Chitarman painted Shah Jahan in 1627–28. The ruler stands on a terrace. He holds a small jewel with his own picture in it. He wears jewels and clothes with patterns. A bright circle of light, called a halo, shines around his head. Small angels like those in European art fly above him. The picture was planned to show his rank. Weavers, jewellers and many other makers made his fine things. Ideas came from many places.

Another page has flowing calligraphy. This is fine, skilled writing. Plants and grazing animals surround it. The writing is by Mir 'Ali Haravi. He is linked with Herat, now in Afghanistan. The writing is from about 1535 to 1545. The painting around it is probably from the 1600s. So an old work got a new setting. Both pages show what the court liked and could pay for. They do not show everyone's life in the empire.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Chitarman painted Shah Jahan in 1627–28. The ruler stands on a terrace. He holds a small jewelled pendant with a picture of himself inside. He wears jewels and patterned clothes. A ring of light called a halo shines around his head. Small angels like those in European art fly above. This picture was planned to show his status. Weavers, jewellers and many other makers made beautiful things for him. The ideas came from many places.

The other page has flowing calligraphy. Calligraphy is careful, skilful writing of letters. Plants and grazing animals surround the letters. The letters were written by Mir 'Ali Haravi. He is linked with Herat, now in Afghanistan. The letters were written around 1535 to 1545. The painting around them was probably done later, in 1600 to 1699. So the old work got a new home. Both pages show what the court liked and had money to pay for, not the lives of everyone in the empire.

write.prompt.source: Explain how the court's support brought different artistic skills together. Use one fact about the workshop and one feature or fact from an album page. Two or three sentences are enough.
write.prompt.back: Explain how a court's support brought different artistic skills together. Use one fact about the workshop and one feature or fact from an album page. 2 or 3 sentences is enough.

write.example.source: In the court's workshop, painters, calligraphers and bookbinders worked on one book. One artist might plan a picture while others added the colour. On the album page, writing by Mir 'Ali Haravi from the 1530s got new painted borders many years later. This shows that the court's money joined the skills of many people. It even joined work from different times.
write.example.back: In the court's workshop, painters, calligraphers and bookbinders worked on the same book. One artist might plan a picture while others painted the colour. On the album page, Mir 'Ali Haravi's writing from the 1530s got a newly painted border many years later. This shows that the court's money brought many people's skills together, and also brought work from different times together.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The empire grew and changed through conquest, treaties and government, so artistic exchange didn't happen between equals; working together at court doesn't show religious harmony across the empire or erase conflict and unequal access to patronage. Religious or regional identities aren't fixed styles, and a painter's name alone doesn't show their religion. No learner is asked to share their religion or identity. The V&A article's many violent illustrations aren't used.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: The empire grew and changed through conquest, treaties and rule, so artistic exchange did not happen between equals. Working together at court doesn't show religions living in harmony across the empire, and doesn't erase conflict or unequal access to patronage. Religious or regional identity is not a fixed art style, and a painter's name alone doesn't tell his religion. No learner is asked to share their own religion or identity. The many violent illustrations in the V&A article are not used.
